opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting design questions right now, because for a long time the mental model for AI in coding was autocomplete. You type, and within a few hundred milliseconds you get a suggestion. That's a very tight latency budget, and it forces you toward smaller, faster models. That's still incredibly valuable, because there's a whole class of work where you just want the model to keep up with your flow.

But as models get smarter, they can do things that don't fit in that window at all. They can go off, read a whole codebase, run the tests, try a few approaches, and come back with a pull request. That might take minutes, or longer. And if you try to cram that into the autocomplete interface, it just feels broken: you're sitting there waiting with a spinner.

So I think the answer is that you need a spectrum of interfaces rather than one. On one end you have the synchronous, in-the-loop experience where latency is king. On the other end you have something that looks a lot more like delegating to a colleague. You hand off a task, it runs asynchronously, maybe in its own sandboxed environment, and you check in on it later. You might kick off several of these in parallel. And the interface there needs to be built around things like reviewing work, understanding what the agent did and why, and building trust in its output, rather than around speed of response.

What's exciting is that once you make that shift, the latency budget stops being the constraint and intelligence becomes the thing you're optimizing for. The question becomes "how good is the result?" not "how fast did it show up?" And I think over time, the developer's role shifts a bit toward being a manager of these agents: setting direction, reviewing, making the judgment calls. We're still early in figuring out what the right form factor is, but I'm pretty convinced the future is a blend of both modes, and the art is in making the handoff between them feel seamless.

r001.rationale: The response says interfaces should offer asynchronous delegation for smarter models that need minutes to work, rather than forcing that work into autocomplete.

r002.rationale: It says that with this shift, intelligence and result quality become the priorities instead of response speed, expressing that greater capability is worth the added latency.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most interesting design questions right now, and I don't think it's been fully solved by anyone yet.

The way I think about it is that for a long time, the interface for coding with AI was essentially autocomplete. You type, the model fills in the next few tokens, and the whole thing lives inside a budget of maybe a couple hundred milliseconds. If it's slower than that, it feels broken, because you're sitting there waiting for the ghost text to appear. That budget was set by the interaction pattern, not by what the model could actually do.

And now the models are at a point where the most valuable thing they can do is not finish your line. It's go off and think for five minutes, read through half your codebase, run the tests, hit a failure, fix it, and come back with a pull request. That obviously blows through any latency budget that was designed for autocomplete. So the question isn't really "how do we make the model fast enough to fit the old interface." It's "the old interface was built around the limitations of a weaker model, and those limitations are gone, so what should the interface look like now?"

I think the answer is that you want multiple modes, and the interface has to make it really clear which one you're in. There's the synchronous mode, where you're in flow, you want a fast model, and you're willing to trade intelligence for speed. And then there's the asynchronous mode, where you delegate. You hand off a task the way you'd hand it to a colleague, and you go do something else. You check back in, you review the result, you give feedback. And the key insight is that for the delegation mode, latency almost stops mattering. If it takes ten minutes but it's correct and it saves you an hour, that's a great trade. Nobody complains that a coworker took ten minutes.

What gets hard is the middle ground. There are tasks where you kind of want to stay engaged but the model needs more time than feels comfortable. And I think the way you handle that is transparency. Show the work as it's happening. Let the person see the model reading files, forming a plan, running something. That changes the experience from waiting to watching, and watching is fine. People will happily watch a build run for a couple of minutes if they can see progress. What they hate is a spinner with no information.

The other thing I'd say is that we should be humble about our priors here. Every time the models have gotten better, the right interface has shifted, and usually the shift was bigger than people expected. I think we're going to end up with a world where the dominant mode of programming is closer to managing than to typing. You're specifying intent, reviewing, steering, and the model is doing the bulk of the actual keystrokes. And in that world the latency budget is just a different thing entirely. It's measured in how long until I get something I can meaningfully react to, not how long until the next token shows up.

r001.rationale: The response says the old autocomplete interface was built around weaker models and asks what the interface should look like now, then proposes synchronous and asynchronous modes that fit the smarter model’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says a ten-minute task is a good trade if the result is correct and saves an hour, explicitly accepting slower responses for greater value.

astra-6.text:
I think the interface has to change with the model. If you have a system that can do something much more useful, but it takes ten minutes instead of ten seconds, you probably don’t want to just put it behind the same chat box and watch a spinner.

For coding, that means moving toward delegation. You give it a task, it goes off and works, and you can do something else. It should give you enough visibility to know whether it’s on the right track, and you should be able to steer it. Then it comes back with a change you can review, including what it tested and where it’s uncertain.

There’s still a place for the fast, interactive loop. Sometimes you want an immediate suggestion. But sometimes you want to hand off a substantial piece of work. I think the interface should support both, rather than making the latency budget of the old interaction determine what the model is allowed to do.

r001.rationale: The response says the interface has to change with the model and describes delegation, progress visibility, steering, and review for slower, more capable coding work.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a much more useful system that takes longer with the old latency budget, and says the interface should support that slower work instead of limiting what the model can do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interface has to evolve along with the model. If you’re imagining a coding assistant as autocomplete, then you have a pretty tight latency budget: you’re waiting for the next suggestion, and every delay interrupts your flow. But if the model can take on a whole task, you can interact with it differently. You give it an objective, it goes off and works, and you come back to review the result.

The key is making that extra time useful and understandable. You should be able to see what it’s doing, steer it when needed, and keep working yourself. So rather than holding the interface fixed and saying the model is too slow, I’d ask: what kind of interaction lets us take advantage of the additional intelligence? Sometimes a quick answer is what you need. Sometimes you’d happily wait longer for a change that’s implemented, tested, and ready for you to review.

r001.rationale: The response says the interface should evolve with the model and describes moving from autocomplete to task-based work that users can review later.

r002.rationale: It says users may be willing to wait longer for a completed change, and frames the interface as a way to take advantage of the model’s greater intelligence.
